body:
## Galaxies you almost cannot see

Most galaxy catalogs stop where the light gets thin. A spiral or elliptical with a bright core is easy. A diffuse patch that never rises much above the night sky is not. Astronomers call the faintest of those patches almost-dark galaxies. They are not empty. They are just extremely dilute in starlight.

Until recently, the clearest examples lived in the Local Group, where proximity lets surveys catch stars that would vanish at greater distance. Analogues should exist farther out. Catching them needs imaging that goes deep enough across a wide field. That is the job Rubin was built for.

## Seven patches around M49

A team led by Minh Ngoc Le at the Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias, with Johan H. Knapen, Zeljko Ivezic, and a large Rubin collaboration, searched Data Preview 2 of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time. The paper, "Rubin LSST DP2 unveils almost-dark galaxies in the Virgo Cluster," went onto arXiv on 16 September 2026 as 2609.19246.

Their hunt centered on the Cosmic Treasure Chest field near M49, the giant elliptical that anchors the Virgo B subcluster. That field spans about 24 square degrees. In the g, r, and i bands the coadds reach surface-brightness limits near the depth expected for the full 10-year survey. Visual inspection turned up seven candidates. The authors label them AD 1 through AD 7, with coordinates such as Rubin J122848.6+085727 for AD 1 and Rubin J122703.1+080018 for AD 7.

Measured at an adopted Virgo distance of about 16.17 Mpc, the seven objects show g-band central surface brightnesses from about 26.9 to 28.5 mag per square arcsecond. Half-light radii run from about 0.6 to 4.6 kpc. Stellar masses sit near 10^6 to 10^7 solar masses. Most have flat Sersic profiles with index below 1. Mean colors near (g-r) of 0.5 point to old, metal-poor stars. None show clear tidal shredding in the images the team presents.

## Why "almost dark" is not the same as ultra-diffuse

Ultra-diffuse galaxies can be large and faint. Almost-dark galaxies sit even fainter, often by a factor of tens in surface brightness at similar size. The seven Virgo finds land among the faintest dwarfs known, closer in properties to Local Group satellites such as Andromeda XXI, XXIII, and XXV than to classic Coma ultra-diffuse galaxies.

AD 7 is the standout. Its half-light radius is about 4.6 kpc, and its central g-band surface brightness is about 28.5 mag per square arcsecond. A single Sersic fit fails, so the team used a core-Sersic model. If the object is real and at Virgo distance, it is among the most extreme low-surface-brightness systems reported in that cluster. The authors flag that AD 7 sits near bright neighbors in a region that may be oversubtracted, and they call for follow-up with a low-surface-brightness-friendly strategy before anyone treats it as settled.

## Distance, gas, and what is still open

Association with Virgo rests on projected distance from M49 (mostly within about 1 Mpc of its virial radius) and on the angular sizes. Push the same objects to twice Virgo's distance and their physical sizes become extreme relative to formation models. Pull them into the foreground near 5 Mpc and individual stars should start to resolve at Rubin's depth. The images stay smooth. That sandwich of arguments favors Virgo membership, with AD 4 near the edge of the virial radius.

ALFALFA gives no HI detection for any of the seven, with an upper limit near 10^7 solar masses at Virgo distance. Except for AD 4, which lies outside the VESTIGE footprint, none show H-alpha either. Red, quiet, and gas-poor is the picture. Background subtraction in DP2 can still clip faint outskirts, so total light and profile shapes may be underestimated. Formal fit errors also understate sky and PSF systematics. Those caveats belong next to the census claim, not after it.

## What Rubin's early data already proves

This is a proof of concept, not a complete catalog of the field. Several of the objects were missed by earlier deep Virgo surveys. One (AD 5) was found independently by another group. Three appear in a recent NGVS catalog as well. The useful sentence is simpler: early Rubin coadds already reach the almost-dark regime outside the Local Group.

The full 10-year LSST will cover about 18,000 square degrees at similar or greater depth. A statistical sample of almost-dark galaxies is what theorists need when they compare the faint end of the luminosity function to warm versus cold dark-matter predictions. Seven objects do not settle that debate. They show the survey can collect the objects the debate needs.

Measured: seven low-surface-brightness candidates around M49 in Rubin DP2, with the sizes, brightnesses, and masses above. Inferred: a Virgo population of Local-Group-like almost-dark galaxies is now reachable in wide-field optical data, and AD 7 is the extreme case that most needs confirmation.
